halaman.alt: Sindi sits outside in the dark and smiles.
teks: A gentle voice spoke to her. “Dear little Sindi,” the voice said. “School is a wonderful place. You will learn many things: to read and write, to sing and dance and to make many friends.”“But for now, Sindi, you must rest. Tomorrow will be beautiful.”

halaman.alt: The moon winks.
teks: Sindi had never seen anything this amazing. She wanted to wake everyone up and show them the talking moon and dancing stars.
But the moon stopped her. “Shhhh, Sindi,”it said. “This is our little secret.” The moon winked.
Sindi returned to bed, comforted by the moon’s wise words, and slept peacefully.

halaman.alt: Sindi and Mama walk to the school.
teks: The time came for school. Mama held Sindi’s hand as they approached the school.
She was confident that the day would be beautiful, because the moon had told her so.
Children were arriving with their mothers and fathers. They all looked excited. Sindi could not wait to make friends.

halaman.alt: Sindi dances and sings with her new school friends.
teks: By lunch time, Sindi loved everything about school.
“I wish the moon could see me now,” she said to herself. “Now I will learn to read. I will learn to write.
But also I will sing and dance!”
And all of Sindi’s new friends danced with her, just like the animals had done. They clapped their hands and sang to her tune.

buku.title: Sindiwe & the Fireflies
buku.subtitle: The Story of Sindiwe Magona
buku.creator: Cheréne Pienaar, Jano Strydom, Tess Gadd
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: There once was a girl named Sindiwe Magona. She had a special gift for stories. At night, little Sindiwe’s grandmother told her magical stories about ogres and giants, animals of the forests and the little creatures of the veld. This was Sindiwe’s favourite time. See how she grows up to live out her own adventures and she travels over oceans to change the world with her stories.

halaman.alt: A young Sindiwe reads a book.
teks: One day a very clever baby was born in Gungululu in the Eastern Cape.
Her name was Sindiwe Magona.
She was the oldest of eight children.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe sits on a log. It is dark and there are stars in the sky.
teks: At night, her grandmother told magical stories about ogres and giants, animals of the forests, great beasts, and little creatures of the veld.
It was Sindiwe’s favourite time.

halaman.alt: Young Sindiwe stands by the chalkboard like a teacher.
teks: Sindiwe loved school and she dreamed about being a teacher.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe is at a party with her family. A man sings to her.
teks: When Sindiwe became a teenager, her family organised a feast to celebrate.
She was given special things to wear and a wise old man sang a praise song to her.
(Blessings, long life! May your ancestors guard you!)

halaman.alt: Sindiwe stands outside a classroom packed full of children.
teks: Sindiwe trained to be a teacher. She was very excited to teach at her first school.
But there weren’t enough schools for black children and they had no desks or books to write in.
This made Sindiwe feel scared. How could she be a good teacher when the children had nowhere to sit?

halaman.alt: Sindiwe wears a maid's uniform. She dusts and and cleans a house.
teks: She left the school to work as a cleaner.
She worked in four different houses. Sometimes the people there treated her badly and Sindiwe became very unhappy.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe is on an aeroplane with her three children.
teks: All this time Sindiwe studied.
Her hard work paid off! She won a scholarship to study at a university in New York.
She and her three small children packed their bags and flew across the sea to the United States of America.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe studies at her desk.
teks: In New York, Sindiwe studied to become a social worker. She wanted to help families make their lives better.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe carries a suitcase. She stands outside the United Nations building.
teks: When she finished studying, the United Nations gave Sindiwe a job.
Most of the countries in the world meet at the United Nations to talk about their problems.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe holds hands with many people of different cultures.
teks: Sindiwe told the world about South Africa, and how hard it was for black people living there.
The people at the United Nations loved to listen to Sindiwe’s stories. They wanted to learn more and more about South Africans.
Perhaps, together, they could help to change things in South Africa.

halaman.alt: Sindiwe packs her suitcase.
teks: She worked at the United Nations for twenty years while her children grew into adults.
But Sindiwe missed the country where she was born. She wanted to tell her stories to the people at home.
So she packed her luggage, got on a plane and flew back over the sea to Cape Town.

halaman.alt: An old Sindiwe reads a story to three children.
teks: Sindiwe’s love for books and stories have helped her write piles and piles of books. And children and grown-ups love to read her stories.
Many people call her Nomabali because she’s always writing, telling and reading stories.

buku.title: Singing the Truth
buku.subtitle: The Story of Miriam Makeba
buku.creator: Jade Mathieson, Louwrisa Blaauw, Bianca de Jong
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Learn about the amazing life of a little girl who grew up to use her gift of singing to help bring freedom to South Africa

halaman.alt: Miriam's mother holds baby Miriam in her arms.
teks: A long time ago, in the vast city of Johannesburg, a baby girl was born. That baby was me. My mom called me Miriam. Miriam Makeba.

halaman.alt: Miriam's mother washes dishes. She carries her baby on her back.
teks: Mom was a sangoma, but she also worked to make other people’s homes neat and clean. It was hard for my mom to earn enough for both of us. She started selling homemade beer to bring in more money.

halaman.alt: Miriam's mother feeds baby Miriam in a jail cell.
teks: The laws of the land said that selling homemade beer was wrong. The police sent my mom to jail for six long months. I was only 18 days old, and needed my mom. So even though I was just a baby, I went to jail too.

halaman.alt: Little Miriam vacuums the carpet. She sings as she goes.
teks: As a little girl I loved to sing. When I was older, I helped my mom clean houses. Singing songs as I worked made the chores go faster and the days seem brighter. Singing made me happier than I can explain.

halaman.alt: Young Miriam holds a microphone and sings in church.
teks: I sang in my church, and this made others happy too. Music has the power to bring people together. When we were singing we felt brave and strong.

halaman.alt: Miriam sings on a professional stage. She is accompanied by a guitarist and a trumpet player.
teks: People said my voice was a gift and my songs were special. I sang with other musicians and our music was heard all over the world.

halaman.alt: In the apartments in Sophiatown, there are many people dancing to music.
teks: My home was Sophiatown, a place of culture and music. Sophiatown, a place where South Africans could make music in harmony and dance together. But the people who ruled the land at the time did not like this togetherness. Those rulers didn’t want black and white people to be friends.

halaman.alt: Miriam wheels her luggage through the airport. She is crying.
teks: I knew it was wrong to treat people differently because of their skin colour. I did not hide my beliefs, and so those people in charge wanted me out of the country. When I was singing in America, I was told I could never return home.

halaman.alt: People from around the world read the newspaper.
teks: People all over the world heard my story. My songs and my story helped many to see how there was no fairness in South Africa for those with black skin. I decided to go on singing and telling the truth about my country, no matter what.

halaman.alt: Miriam sings for a king and queen.
teks: The world loved my music and I was welcomed in many countries. I won awards and sang for important people all over the globe. My life was good, but something was missing. I could not sing in my home country, and people there were not free.

halaman.alt: Miriam dances with Nelson Mandela.
teks: Then a wonderful day dawned when Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa. New people were in charge and the unfair laws belonged to the past. I finally went home with new hope in my heart.

halaman.alt: Miriam dances and sings on stage. People of all colours dance in the audience.
teks: After that I could sing in a free, fair country. People of different skin colours could enjoy music together. I helped make this happen because I was brave and strong. I sang the truth in all of my songs.

buku.title: Sizwe's Smile
buku.creator: Vianne Venter, Genevieve Terblanche, Lauren Rycroft
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Today Sizwe learns that a smile is something you can give away without losing it.

halaman.alt: Sizwe sits on his bed. He is smiling.
teks: It had been raining for days, and everyone was grumpy. Everyone except Sizwe, who woke up with a smile every morning.
“Yoh! Sizwe! That smile is magic!” said Gogo. “Is it for me?” Sizwe clapped his hand over his mouth. “But it’s MY smile, Gogo,” he whispered.

halaman.alt: Sizwe and his mother look in the mirror. They are both smiling.
teks: His mother laughed. “Sizwe! A smile is something you can give away without losing it. Look!”
She lifted him up to the mirror. There was his smile, just as bright as before.

halaman.alt: Zanele and her dog look out the window. Zanele is not smiling.
teks: It was time to go out. Mama buttoned up Sizwe’s raincoat, and off they went, through the rain, to the library.
Down the street, Sizwe’s best friend Zanele stood at the window of her house, looking sadly at the rain.
Sizwe felt his smile creeping, creeping up. Before he knew it, his smile LEAPT out, and flew across the garden to Zanele.

halaman.alt: Zanele holds up the letter. She is smiling at the postman.
teks: Zanele held on tightly to the smile – it was far too precious to let it get away.
As Sizwe walked away to the library, Zanele’s doorbell rang. It was the postman, with a letter from her favourite cousin.
Zanele was so happy, that the smile bounced up, and beamed out at the postman. “Thank you, Mister Postman!” she said.

halaman.alt: The postman smiles at the barking dog.
teks: Zanele’s smile was the brightest thing the postman had seen all morning. It kept him warm as he trudged off through the rain.
He came to a big house. Inside the gate, a dog was spinning around in circles, barking, barking, barking. He was so silly, that the postman couldn’t help smiling.
The smile bounced through the gate with a glitter of glee.

halaman.alt: The dog wags its tail. The old man smiles.
teks: The dog stopped barking. He pricked up his ears and wagged his tail. Then he turned and ran back to the house with the precious, warm smile.
A bent old man opened the door. “Oh, no! You can’t come inside. You’re all wet!” he told the dog. But right away, the smile beamed up at the old man.

halaman.alt: The old man and the dog walk together. Mrs Makabela stands at the pedestrian crossing. She is not smiling.
teks: The old man stood a little straighter. “Eish,” he said, “Who cares if it’s raining? Let’s go for a walk, boy!” And off they went, splashing in the puddles.
There, at the zebra crossing, stood grumpy Mrs Makabela, the traffic cop. She looked cold, and wet, and miserable.
The old man knew just what to do. “Morning, Mrs Makabela!” he called, and smiled his biggest, brightest smile.
But Mrs Makabela... did not smile back.

halaman.alt: Mrs Makabela is smiling. The children cross the road.
teks: Standing in the rain for days can make a face sad, sad, sad. But a smile is a magical thing and, by now, the smile was so strong, and so bright, that it was very hard to keep inside. It didn’t work right away, but bit by tiny bit, it began to creep out until, at last...!
A great, big smile lit up Mrs Makabela’s face!
The school bell rang, and children ran to cross the road. Mrs Makabela put up her sign, and smiled, and smiled, at each and every child.

halaman.alt: Everyone is smiling!
teks: The children smiled at their moms and dads, and their gogos and tatas and brothers and sisters. They smiled at the bus driver and the greengrocer, and Mme Makau, who went off to smile at her husband, who smiled at the mayor...
The smiles leapt and rolled and beamed and gleamed until EVERYONE was smiling and giggling and laughing out loud in the rain.

halaman.alt: Sizwe and his mother are at the library. Sizwe is not smiling.
teks: In the library, everything was quiet except for the sound of the rain. “It’s time to go,” said Sizwe’s mother, closingher book.“Aw, mom!” said Sizwe, who had run out of smiles.

halaman.alt: Everyone is in the street. They are all smiling.
teks: But as they stepped out into the street...
WHAT A SIGHT!
Everyone in town was there!
Everyone!
And they were ALL smiling!

halaman.alt: The sun is shining. Sizwe is smiling.
teks: The smiles bounced around and beamed at Sizwe. They warmed him, and tickled him, and crept up, up, up from his toes... to the TOP of his head. He was so full of happiness that the smile burst out, brilliant and beaming bright.
And something changed. The dark, gloomy, rainy afternoon didn’t seem so dark anymore.
Could it be...? YES!
The clouds parted, and the warm sun shone down on them, with the biggest, brightest, most brilliant smile of all.

buku.title: Sleepy Mr Sloth
buku.creator: Graham Paterson, Paul Kennedy, Nick Mulgrew
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: He’s quite good at climbing. He knows how to swing. But sleeping’s his favourite, favourite thing!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth is sleepy and yawning.
teks: One day, Mr Sloth came to visit. He said:
I’m sleepy! I need a good branch for a bed!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth starts climbing the tree.
teks: I’m quite good at climbing. I know how to swing.
But sleeping’s my favourite, favourite thing!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. Is that a big ear nearby?
teks: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.
And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?

halaman.alt: A giraffe bites Mr Sloth by mistake!
teks: Oh no, Mr Sloth! A giraffe’s eating there!
He might think you’re lunch and start nibbling your hair!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There are a few bees flying around.
teks: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.
And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?

halaman.alt: Bees fly out of a beehive around Mr Sloth!
teks: Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a beehive right there!
You’ll never get sleep with those bees everywhere!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There is a tail nearby.
teks: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.
And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth grabs snake by mistake!
teks: Oh no, Mr Sloth, that’s a snake over there!
Not a branch! Poor old snake. You gave him quite a scare.

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There are feet nearby.
teks: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.
And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?

halaman.alt: A hadeda is squawking loudly there!
teks: Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a bird squawking there!
You’ll never get sleep with that noise in the air!

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth climbs to the top of the tree and smiles.
teks: Try climb one more branch, Mr Sloth! they all said.
And that branch was just the right one for his bed.

halaman.alt: Mr Sloth and the animals are all sleeping nicely in the tree together.
teks: The bird and the snake, the giraffe and each bee
were happy to have Mr Sloth in their tree.

buku.title: Springloaded
buku.creator: Thea Nicole de Klerk, Sam Wilson, Chenél Ferreira
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Neo’s father is an inventor. When he invents a helicopter hat and flies away, Neo decides to make an invention of her own.

halaman.alt: An inventor sits at his desk making something. His daughter, Neo and her cat watch him work. He has made a hat with a propeller on top.
Neo waves goodbye as her father flies up in the air wearing his new invention.
With her father gone, Neo is bored. She walks around aimlessly.
Neo has an idea. She will make something too. While her cat sleeps, she reads Science books and makes plans to build springy shoes.
Neo wears her springy shoes and a red cape. She bounches up in the air.
She bounces on the pavement.
She bounces high above the buildings.
She bounces across the world.
She bounces high above the clouds.
She starts to come back down to earth. Her father is waiting to catch her.
Her father catches her. He looks at her new springy shoes.
Neo, her cat and her father are all wearing springy shoes and bouncing in space.

buku.title: Thato's Birthday Surprise
buku.creator: Jodi Houareau, Brad Cuzen, Corinne Lamoral-Rosmarin
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: It is one week until Thato’s Birthday. His mama tells him he will have a big surprise. What will it be?

halaman.alt: Thato points to the calendar on his bedroom wall.
teks: It is one week until Thato’s birthday.
That’s seven whole days!

halaman.alt: Thato eats his breakfast. Mama says he will get a big surprise for his birthday.
teks: His mama says: “Your birthday present will be a BIG surprise!”
Thato wonders: what will it be?

halaman.alt: Thato flies in the sky. He has wings strapped to his arms.
teks: On Monday Thato thinks:
Maybe I will get giant wings so I can fly high in the sky like a bird...”

halaman.alt: The house next door is a giant cake!
teks: On Tuesday Thato thinks:
“Maybe I will have a birthday cake as big as a house!”

halaman.alt: Thato flies in a rocket through space.
teks: On Wednesday Thato thinks:
“Maybe I will get a rocket ship to whizz up to the moon.

halaman.alt: Thato wears goggles and flippers. He swims under the ocean.
teks: On Thursday Thato thinks:
“Maybe I will get fins so I can swim under the water like a fish.”

halaman.alt: Thato is on a soccer field. He holds a trophy high in the air.
teks: On Friday Thato thinks:
“Maybe I will get magic soccer boots and score a thousand goals!”

halaman.alt: Thato wears a crown. He opens a box which sparkles with jewels.
teks: On Saturday Thato thinks:
“Maybe I will get a key that opens a box filled with treasure!”

halaman.alt: Mama opens the door for Thato.
teks: On Sunday it is Thato’s birthday.
Mama smiles and says: “Come and see your surprise!”

halaman.alt: Thato's brother gets out of a taxi. He carries his luggage.
teks: It is the best present ever.
Thato’s big brother Kudzai has come to visit all the way from the big city!

halaman.alt: Thato's brother picks Thato up and hugs him.
teks: Thato smiles and smiles and his big brother lifts him up in the air and hugs him.
Kudzai asks:“What do you want to do for your birthday, little brother?”

halaman.alt: Thato thinks of his wings, his cake, flying through space, swimming, playing soccer and hunting for treasure.
teks: And Thato knows exactly what they will do the whole day long.

buku.title: The Best Thing Ever
buku.creator: Melissa Fagan, Lauren Nel, Stefania Origgi
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Muzi loves to build with his toys. But when he leaves them behind to travel to uGogo’s house, he discovers something very special about the world. And he learns something new about himself.

halaman.alt: Muzi looks at the impressive tower he has made with wooden blocks.
teks: Muzi loves to build things.
He dreams of building the best thing ever.

halaman.alt: Muzi has built a shelter for his toys. It is a blanket tied to a door handle. His mother opens the door. The shelter falls apart.
teks: Once he built a shelter for his toys.
But it wasn’t the best thing ever.

halaman.alt: Muzi builds a bridge with his blocks. One part falls down under the weight of his toy animals.
teks: Yesterday he built a bridge for his animals.
It was a good thing. But not the best...

halaman.alt: Muzi closes the door to his bedroom where all his toys are packed away. He carries a backpack.
teks: Today Muzi is going to visit uGogo.
He is sad. Without his toys, how can he build the best thing ever?

halaman.alt: Muzi and his mother stand at the bus stop. They point to a man and his overflowing trolley of recyclable objects.
teks: At the bus stop, Muzi is amazed.
He sees red things and blue things.
Small things and big things.
New things and old things.

halaman.alt: Muzi sits on his mother's lap inside the bus. He sees clouds in the shape of a house.
teks: Muzi has a new idea for building the best thing ever.

halaman.alt: Muzi kneels down and picks up objects in the road: bottle tops and cans and ice cream sticks...
teks: On the road to uGogo’s, Muzi finds many things.
Long things and short things.
Round things and square things.

halaman.alt: Muzi stands by the river. He notices leaves and twigs and stones.
teks: By the riverside, Muzi finds more things.
Soft things and pointy things.
Green things and brown things.

halaman.alt: Muzi and his mother arrive at Gogo's shack. They carry shopping bags filled with Muzi's found objects.
teks: Look, Muzi! We are here.

halaman.alt: Muzi's mother and Gogo bake bread. Muzi builds in the corner using dough and his newfound things.
teks: While uGogo bakes for the hungry travellers...
Muzi builds.

halaman.alt: Muzi presents his sculpture to Gogo. It is a house made from dough and all his found objects.
teks: Look Gogo, a new house for you.
Oh, Muzi, laughs Gogo.
This is the best thing ever!

halaman.alt: The house is a beautiful mix of colours and textures using bottle tops, sticks, matchboxes and more.
teks: Gogo, Gogo! says Muzi. The world is full of toys. Look what I can build.

buku.title: The Elephant in the Room
buku.creator: Sam Wilson, Michael Tymbios, Thomas Pepler
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Lindi finds a very large elephant in her room. But is it really there if no one else believes in it?

halaman.alt: An elephant stands inside a room.
teks: One morning, Lindi found an elephant in her room.
“Look!” she called. “There’s an elephant in my room!”
“No there isn’t,” her mother called back. “Elephants don’t live in houses. Everybody knows that.”
The elephant yawned.

halaman.alt: In the kitchen, the table is set with breakfast things. The elephant sticks its trunk into the milk jug.
teks: At breakfast, Lindi’s dad asked her to pass the milk.
“I can’t,” said Lindi. “The elephant drank it all.”
“There isn’t an elephant,” said her dad. “Elephants don’t live in the city. Everybody knows that.”
The elephant burped.

halaman.alt: The elephant stands in front of the classroom. He has '1 + 1' drawn on his hide.
teks: At school, the teacher grumbled, “What’s wrong with this chalkboard? It’s all wrinkly!”
“That’s not the chalkboard. That’s my elephant!” said Lindi.
“There are no elephants at school,” said the teacher. “Everybody knows that.”
The elephant ate the teacher’s sandwiches.

halaman.alt: Lindi stands in the playground and cries. The elephant has damaged the swings.
teks: At break-time, the elephant followed Lindi to the playground.
He knocked over the swings by mistake.
“Go away!” said Lindi. “You’re not real and you shouldn’t be here! Everybody knows that!”
The elephant drooped. He walked away, wiping his eyes with his trunk.

halaman.alt: Lindi looks into the distance with a pair of binoculars.
teks: After school, Lindi couldn’t see the elephant anywhere.
“Elephant!” she called. “Where are you?

halaman.alt: It is dark. Lindi sits alone outside her house.
teks: Lindi went home without him.
She felt lonely.
So she went outside, and sat on the steps, and waited.
And waited.
And waited.

halaman.alt: It is light. Lindi sees the elephant coming down the road.
teks: And then ... she saw a trunk.
And tusks.
And ears.
The elephant was coming down the road!

halaman.alt: Lindi is reunited with the elephant.
teks: She ran up and hugged him.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t mean it! I know you’re real. You’re my elephant.”

halaman.alt: Lindi rides on the elephant's back.
teks: The elephant lifted her up and put her on his back, and she rode down the street.
She waved to her neighbours.
“Hello, Mr Green! Hello, Mrs Green!”
“Look at Lindi!” said Mr Green. “How did she get up there? Maybe she grew!”
“Don’t be silly,” said Mrs Green. “Little girls don’t grow that high. Everybody knows that.”

halaman.alt: Lindi and the elephant swim in the lake.
teks: The elephant took Lindi to the lake, and she slid down his trunk like it was a slide.
“Wheeeee!” she shrieked.
They played all afternoon, laughing and splashing and spraying each other with water.

halaman.alt: Lindi is in her bed. The elephant stands outside her bedroom window.
teks: That night, the elephant tucked her into bed.
“Good night, Elephant,” said Lindi. “Thank you for a lovely day.”
He patted her head, and curled up to sleep outside her window.

halaman.alt: Lindi faces her elephant.
teks: “Elephants are the best friends in the world,” Lindi said to herself. “Nobody knows that, except for me and my elephant.”

buku.title: The Lion Who Wouldn't Try
buku.creator: Nick Mulgrew, André Kieswetter, Liza Esterhuyse
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction

buku.title: There Must be a Rainbow
buku.creator: Thulisizwe Mamba, Sinomonde Ngwane, Nerissa Govender
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: In this delightful tale of hope, Jabulile’s dream of helping people comes true after a terrible storm hits the Valley.

halaman.alt: The sun rises over a small village in the hills.
teks: Nestled in the Kingdom of the Zulu is a magnificent place called the Valley.

halaman.alt: Jabulile is happy.
teks: A little girl called Jabulile lives here. Jabulile was always a happy child. She was also curious, and full of questions about life.
Everything fascinated her.

halaman.alt: Jabulile and her mom and dad are happy, standing in a field.
teks: Jabulile’s father was a mielie farmer. Her mother was a teacher. They taught her to dream big dreams. Jabulile’s biggest dream was to help people.

halaman.alt: Jabulile thinks of a rainbow and is happy.
teks: Everyone in the village was Jabulile’s friend, especially the elders. They taught her about the wise men and women who once lived in the Valley. Jabulile also wanted to be wise.

halaman.alt: Jabulile and a man spot a big storm coming.
teks: One awful day, the clouds began to gather over the Valley. Everything grew dark and grey. An ugly storm swept over the land.

halaman.alt: The big storm blows the tops off the houses.
teks: Great gusts of wind blew the roofs off the huts. All the animals lost their homes. It was a very sad day.

halaman.alt: Jabulile cheers up the sad villagers.
teks: The village folk cried, “What shall we do now?”
“All the crops are ruined!” cried the farmers.
“Our homes are gone!” said the elders.
All hope seemed lost. But Jabulile remembered something her wise father once told her.

halaman.alt: She points to the rainbow behind the clouds.
teks: Jabulile started speaking to the villagers. “The storm only hurts us,” she said, “because of the way we choose to see it. If you look up the sun is shining again. It is a new day.
“After every storm, there must be a rainbow!” she shouted excitedly.

halaman.alt: A huge rainbow comes out.
teks: Just then a glorious rainbow appeared in the sky.

halaman.alt: The villagers are happy again.
teks: The villagers saw the rainbow and they began to smile. It stood as a promise that the storm was over.

halaman.alt: Jabulile smiles as the rainbow stretch across the horizon and over the village.
teks: The villagers rebuilt their homes. Farmers planted new crops. The grass grew greener than ever before.

halaman.alt: The sun rises once again over the village in the peaceful valley.
teks: Once again there was hope and happiness in the Valley.

buku.title: Together We're Strong
buku.subtitle: The Story of Albertina Sisulu
buku.creator: Liesl Jobson, Alice Toich, Nazli Jacobs
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: From the day she was born to the day she died, Albertina Sisulu lived a life of love and sacrifice. A brave girl who rode a horse, she was a blessing to her family, to her community and to South Africa. This story of a unique and powerful woman, who stood up for her beliefs no matter what, will inspire and enchant.

halaman.alt: Ma Monikazi holds baby Nontsikelelo in her arms.
teks: One harsh winter, many people in the land were sick. Ma Monikazi’s cheeks burned. Sweat dripped from her body. She wanted to hold the icy grass to her face to cool down. Under her blanket she held her belly and sang to the baby inside her: “Be strong, little one. Winter’s not long. Be brave, little one. Together we’re strong!”
Her stomach growled when the baby’s powerful kicks woke her at night. She ate the leftover meat in the cooking pot, hungry for life.

One bright night the moon was bigger, fatter and pinker than ever. Her breath came fast. The baby was ready. The aunties in the birthing room rubbed her back and warmed the water. When Monikazi held her beautiful daughter in her arms, she knew she was a special girl, a fighter.
What a blessing! Her name is Nontsikelelo. She will be the mother of all blessings.

halaman.alt: The women cook food for the family. Baby Ntsiki sits on the floor eating some of the chicken off a plate.
teks: Nontsikelelo was beautiful and strong with crinkling black button eyes. She loved her older brother, Mcengi. He made her laugh and so the laughter spread. She loved to eat meat before she had teeth. Her favourite aunt always kept a little portion on the side of her plate for Ntsiki. Mcengi chased the chickens that scratched in the garden where Ma Monikazi grew spinach and squash to feed her family. Ntsiki ran after him as her legs grew strong.

Ma Monikazi had another baby boy, Velaphi, and another, Qudalele. Finally another sister, Nomyaleko. Little Ntsiki folded napkins and washed the baby clothes. She swept the house and fed the fire. She picked up her baby brother when he cried and tickled him till he laughed.
She taught them to sing: “Be strong, little one. Winter is gone. Be brave, little one. Together we’re strong!”

halaman.alt: Ntsiki pets a horse in the field.
teks: Qingqiwe, her grandfather, raised horses. His favourite was Shishi, a glossy black mare. As soon as Ntsiki was old enough, he hoisted her on to the saddle in front of him. His strong arms reached around her. He laced the reins through her fingers.

He taught her to talk softly to Shishi, to groom her with a hard bristled brush. When she stroked its glossy coat, Albertina whispered, “You are the most beautiful creature. Thank you for letting me ride on your back.”

Her father, Bonilizwe, came home from the mines at Christmas. Ntsiki pulled herself up onto Shishi’s broad back. She rode out to meet him at the bus stop. Ntsiki sat tall and straight. Her knees held firm. She handled the reins with gentle fingers.
How proud Bonilizwe was of his daughter. The biggest smile Ntsiki had ever seen covered her father’s face.

halaman.alt: Ntsiki is at school. She chooses the English name Albertina.
teks: On her sixth birthday she went to school. “You must choose an English name,” said the Presbyterian teacher, but Ntsiki liked her own name. “Why do I need a new name?” she asked. The teacher scowled and read the names aloud: “Adah, Agnes, Albertina, Anna.” What did they mean? Ntsiki liked the long name best. Al-ber-ti-na! The name had rhythm. Al-ber-ti-na! The name had bounce. Albertina was a name you didn’t mess with.

When her cousin married a handsome man from a nearby town, Albertina was chosen as an umkhapi. The maid of honour! Weeks before the wedding, she stitched her isikhakha, the short traditional skirt, and threaded bright beads onto her amatikiti. Her mother gave her the white flag and said, “You have a big job, my blessing.”

At the bend in the road Albertina waved the flag, then turned Shishi back, leading everybody from miles around to the ceremony. People would gossip if she made a mistake, but the guests lined the road. They ululated and sang. They threw down flowers for the horse and the girl.

halaman.alt: Albertina and her friend, Betty study Maths by the light of a candle.
teks: Her mother was often sick and needed Albertina to look after the home. In her last year of primary school, Albertina was the oldest pupil in the school. She was chosen to be the head girl and wore her badge with pride.
Her best friend, Betty, told her about a competition, saying, “You must apply, my clever friend.” “What is the prize?” asked Albertina, growing curious.
“A scholarship to high school!” said Betty. “You must apply. You’ll win it, for sure.

”Albertina studied until the candle burned down. She practised sums. She practised spelling. She sharpened her pencils and gave her shoes an extra shine. Next morning she passed Shishi in her paddock. The horse whinnied and stamped the ground.

halaman.alt: Albertina gets full marks on her Maths test.
teks: The test began. Albertina’s fingers shook. The sums were tricky. Her mouth went dry. Her hand cramped on her pencil but she continued. “Well done, Albertina!” said her teacher at the end. The important official arrived and called the top two students to the stage. “Well done to Albertina for full marks,” he said, “but you are too old. The scholarship goes to...”
Albertina tried not to cry. “That’s unfair,” shouted Betty, hopping with fury. “That wasn’t in the rules!” How would Albertina go to high school now? She dragged her feet all the way home.

The teacher wrote to the newspaper about the unfair decision. Brother Joe at the Catholic Mission station read the story over his breakfast. He cracked his boiled egg with an extra flourish. He pushed the newspaper across the table to Father Bernard. He didn’t like the story one bit either.

halaman.alt: The village has a big party for Albertina.
teks: Soon enough there was a scholarship for Albertina. Mariazell near Matatiele was a long way from Xolobe, but the whole village erupted. Their home girl was off to high school. She would make them proud. They threw a party like no other. The women brewed the sorghum beer and lit the fires. They slaughtered chickens and stirred up pots of meat. Albertina smiled till her face ached.

She packed her brown suitcase and polished her shoes again. Before setting off on the bus to Matatiele, she said goodbye to Shishi. Albertina brushed her coat and stroked her wiry mane. She whispered all her questions into the horse’s silky ear: What if I get lost? Will I make new friends? Will I still be clever so far from home? Shishi whinnied and stamped the ground.

halaman.alt: Albertina waits for the school bus.
teks: School days started well before sunrise. The girls washed quickly in the cold water and swept the dormitories before Mass. The milky porridge was never quite enough; the stew not as tasty as Aunty’s back home. But Albertina studied hard. She played netball on sunny afternoons.

In her school holidays Albertina worked at the mission station. She rubbed and scrubbed against the zinc washboard. She boiled sheets in copper tubs, then wound them through the wringer. She hoed and tilled the school garden but missed her family. Who was telling her brothers and sisters funny stories? Who wiped their eyes when they cried? Who tickled them until they laughed?
Albertina loved the nuns who taught her. Could she become a holy sister? “But nuns earn no salary,” said Father Bernard. “Perhaps you should become a nurse? You’ll be paid while you study.”

halaman.alt: Albertina is a nurse. She cares for a patient in the hospital.
teks: Albertina took a train to Johannesburg. She bought a smart white uniform, new navy shoes and a shiny red fountain pen. Sick people came all day to the hospital. She cleaned their wounds with careful fingers. She held the old people gently. When the babies cried, she sang: “Be strong, little one. Winter’s not long. Be brave, little one. Together we’re strong!

Some nights Albertina worked till dawn. She looked out the window and thought of her family. Were the children hungry? Did they go to school? Who was riding Shishi? She remembered the dark green spinach. She missed the scent of the earth. There was no vegetable garden here. There was nowhere for a horse.

Albertina never went to parties. She saved every shilling. On her days off she learned to play tennis. Whoosh! Plop! She whacked the ball across the net. Always, she wished for a little more money to send home.

halaman.alt: Albertina marries Walter Sisulu.
teks: Walter Sisulu was a brave and clever man who dreamed of freedom for South Africa. His big smile captured Albertina’s eye. They walked together down the city streets. Her delicate hand rested on his arm. Walter wanted Albertina to be the mother of his children.

Bright ribbons decorated the Bantu Men’s Social Centre on their wedding day. Albertina’s long-sleeved dress had a swirling train of lace. Many friends blessed their special day. Albertina planted flowers in her little garden. Within a year, Max was born. Albertina had become a mother. One day people would call her the mother of the nation.

Max had his mother’s black button eyes and his father’s round chin. He was the hope for their future. Albertina wanted to fight for a new South Africa, so that Max could be free. When he cried, she sang: “Be strong, little one. Winter’s not long. Be brave, little one. Together we’re strong!”

halaman.alt: Albertina kneels by the trampled flowers on the ground. A policeman stands over her.
teks: Police came in the middle of the night, banging on the door. Albertina scolded the men who messed up her house. “How rude you are!” she said, “trampling mud inside my home.”

In the morning Albertina’s favourite flowers lay crushed beneath their footprints. She remembered chasing the chickens from her vegetable garden back in Xolobe and set about replanting her garden. The earth, she knew, would recover.
She would support her husband who kept many secrets and hid from the police.

halaman.alt: Albertina leads a women's march outside the Union Buildings.
teks: She joined the women and worked to organise a march to Pretoria. The women refused to carry a pass. They sang, “Wathint’ abafazi; wathint’ imbokodo! You strike a woman; you strike a rock!”
Many hard years followed after Walter’s arrest. He was jailed on Robben Island for 26 years. Albertina, also, was sent to jail many times. Often she was scared. Often she was lonely.

But even on the darkest nights, she could see a sliver of moon through the window in her cell. She sang the song that Ma Monikazi sang before she was born: “Be strong, little one. Winter’s not long. Be brave, little one. Together we’re strong!”

buku.title: Tortoise Finds His Home
buku.creator: Maya Fowler, Katrin Coetzer, Damian Gibbs
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Tortoise sets off in search of his house. Along the way, he meets new friends to help him. But the sky is darkening, and lightning flashes in the distance. Will Tortoise find his house in time?

halaman.alt: Tortoise passes Snail in the veld.
teks: One day Tortoise was walking through the veld.
He was searching and searching. He gazed into the distance and squinted at the grass.
“Are you looking for something?” Snail asked.
“Yes, I’m looking for my house. Have you seen it?”

halaman.alt: Snail travels on Tortoise's back.
teks: “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”
She climbed onto Tortoise’s shell. Tortoise walked on with Snail on his back.
They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.

halaman.alt: Sparrow perches on a branch. Tortoise and Snail pass him.
teks: “Are you looking for something?” asked Sparrow.
“Yes, we're looking for Tortoise's house. Have you seen it?”
“No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”

halaman.alt: Snail sits on Tortoise's back. Sparrow flies ahead of them. There is a ladybird on a dandelion in the distance.
teks: Sparrow flapped his wings and he whizzed away.
“You’re going too fast!” called Tortoise.
“Alright, then I’ll hop on too.”
Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow perched on his shell. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.

halaman.alt: Ladybird sits on a dandelion stem. Tortoise, Snail and Sparrow pass him.
teks: “Are you looking for something?” asked Ladybird.
“Yes, we’re looking for Tortoise’s house. Have you seen it?”

halaman.alt: Snail, Sparrow and Ladybird travel on Snail's back.
teks: “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”
Ladybird hopped onto Tortoise’s shell. Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird sitting on his back.
They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.
A breeze started to blow.

halaman.alt: The animals find Mouse. He is making a daisy chain.
teks: “Are you looking for something?” asked Mouse.
“Yes, Mouse, I’m looking for my house. Have you seen it?”
“No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”

halaman.alt: Mouse climbs on Tortoise's back with the others. The wind blows the leaves and the daisy chain.
teks: Mouse jumped onto Tortoise’s back.
Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse on his back.
They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.
The wind swept the leaves off the ground and swirled them around Tortoise.

halaman.alt: Tortoise walks with Mouse, Snail, Sparrow and Ladybird on his back.
teks: The wind got stronger and stronger. The sky turned dark.
“Oh, where is my house?” Tortoise sighed.
Thunder roared in the hills. Lightning flashed in the distance. Drip, drip came the rain.
“Oh, where is Tortoise’s house?” asked Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse.

halaman.alt: The wind gets stronger. The rain threatens. The animals all fly off Tortoise's back.
teks: The wind whirled and whipped and blew Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse right off Tortoise’s back.

halaman.alt: The hail comes down. Tortoise curls up in his shell. The other animals stand nearby.
teks: “Eek!” squeaked Tortoise with a fright, and he shrank back into his shell.
It was warm and cosy inside.
“Oh, here is my house!”

halaman.alt: Mouse, Ladybird, Snail and Sparrow take shelter underneath Tortoise's shell.
teks: “Oh, here is Tortoise’s house!”

buku.title: Walking Together
buku.creator: Jade Mathieson, Louwrisa Blaauw, Bianca de Jong
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: A walk to the clinic doesn’t have to be dull, when there are so many wonderful things to see on the way.

halaman.alt: A mother and her young daughter walk away from their rondawel.
teks: When we go walking and the road is long, we’ll walk together singing a song.

halaman.alt: They walk far down the road. They walk towards the hills.
teks: I am with you and you are with me.
A journey is fun with our family.

halaman.alt: They see a mother hen with a chick under her wing.
teks: I’ll keep you cosy like a mother hen.
She keeps her chicks warm under her wing.

halaman.alt: They see a man walking in the rain. He wears a traditional straw hat.
teks: If the rain starts to fall down from the sky, like that good hat I’ll keep your face dry.

halaman.alt: The mother and child stand under a rock and watch the rain fall.
teks: If storm clouds get angry and grumble and moan, be brave, why cry?
You’re not alone.

halaman.alt: They see a big waterfall.
teks: We’re walking together so we never get bored.
Look up! Look around!
See where we’ve explored!

halaman.alt: They see a donkey carrying sticks on its back. It also wears a traditional straw hat!
teks: If you see something that’s funny to see, I don’t want to miss it.
Please share it with me!

halaman.alt: They arrive at the clinic building.
teks: If your feet start to hurt from the distance we’ve passed, don’t worry, we’ve made it!
Here’s the clinic at last.

halaman.alt: The clinic sister check's the girl's heart, ears and throat.
teks: We all need to check our throat, lungs and ears.
Get strong as you grow, it’s no reason for tears.

halaman.alt: The clinic sister checks her mother's blood pressure.
teks: Do you think it’s scary?
Here, hold my hand.
She’ll check your blood pressure with this clever armband.

halaman.alt: The mother and daughter leave the clinic. Mother is carrying a bag of medicine. They are both smiling.
teks: They give us our medicine, tell us what we should know, to keep us all healthy.
Now back home we go.

halaman.alt: It is night time. Mother tucks the little girl into her bed.
teks: It’s okay to be tired, there’s so much we’ve seen.
Now it’s your bedtime.
Sleep well and sweet dreams.

buku.title: What if
buku.creator: Julie Ann Smith-Belton, MaryAn Hampton, Cristy Zinn
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Nandi is wondering all sorts of strange things about the world. And it begins with a simple question: What if…?

halaman.alt: A little girl sits outside on the steps of her house. She is dreaming.
teks: Nandi sat on the blue steps of her house.

halaman.alt: There are dream bubbles, birds and coloured shapes all over.
teks: She was wondering...

halaman.alt: Nandi jumps high above her house.
teks: What if jelly beans made you jump really high?
You could get to school in one big leap!

halaman.alt: Nandi talks to two chickens and a goat.
teks: What if goats and chickens could talk?
Would they tell good jokes?

halaman.alt: Nandi blasts off in a rocket ship.
teks: What if houses were rocket ships?
Your family could go on holidays to the moon!

halaman.alt: Nandi sits at the table holding a knife and fork. There is a hamburger on the table.
teks: What if no one had to cook? What if supper just arrived on the table?
(And it was always your favourite.)

halaman.alt: Nandi eats an ice lolly.
teks: What if ice-lollies never melted?
They could last all summer.

halaman.alt: Tigers, elephants, books and their characters swirl around Nandi's head.
teks: What if the pictures in books flew around your head when Dad read to you?

halaman.alt: Nandi wears pink gum boots and runs very fast.
teks: What if my pink gumboots were magical?
I could run faster than my big brother!

halaman.alt: Nandi squeezes her eyes shut.
teks: What if you squeezed your eyes shut and...

halaman.alt: Nandi sits outside on the steps of her house. She is still dreaming. Her brother stands behind her.
teks: “Nandi, what are you doing?” asked Nandi’s big brother.
Nandi sat back on the step with a big smile on her face.

halaman.alt: Nandi smiles.
teks: “Just wondering,” she said.

buku.title: What is it?
buku.creator: Kate Sidley, Robyn Penn, Ann Roberts
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: What is it? It isn’t like me. Do you think it’s dangerous?

halaman.alt: A group of strange-looking animals spot a grey blob in the distance.
teks: What is it?

halaman.alt: The animal that looks like a mixture of a crocodile and an elephant asks: "What is it?"
teks: What is it? It hasn't got a trunk. It's not like me.

halaman.alt: The animal that looks like a mixture of a monkey and a rat asks: "What is it?"
teks: What is it? It hasn’t got a tail. It’s not like me.

halaman.alt: The animal that looks like a mixture of an owl and a sheep asks: "What is it?"
teks: What is it? Ugh! Where are its feathers? It’s not like me.

halaman.alt: A mother and baby buck with claws ask: "What is it?"
teks: What is it? Look at those tiny feet. It’s not like us.

halaman.alt: The crocodile-elephant asks: "Do you think it's dangerous?"
teks: Do you think it’s dangerous?

halaman.alt: The monkey-rat asks: "Do you think it wants to eat us?"
teks: Do you think it wants to eat us?

halaman.alt: The grey blob sneezes.
teks: Achoo! Achoo!

halaman.alt: All of the animals open their eyes wide in fear.
teks: Aargh! Eek! Run!

halaman.alt: The animals run away. A  baby human crawls towards them. The grey blob is her shadow.
teks: It's chasing us!

halaman.alt: The baby buck walks towards the baby human.
teks: Be careful. Come back.

halaman.alt: The baby buck and the baby human rub their noses together in greeting.
teks: What is it?
It's a baby, just like me!

buku.title: When I Grow Up
buku.creator: Simóne van der Spuy, Michele Fry, Jennifer Jacobs
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: I don’t know what I want to be when I grow up. Can you help me choose?

halaman.alt: A young girl stands and holds a sunflower. Her dog sits in the corner.
teks: What do I want to be when I grow up?

halaman.alt: The girl wears ballet clothes and practises her dance steps.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a dancer and dance on a stage.

halaman.alt: The girl wears yellow gumboots and holds a fireman's hose. Her dog stands next to her.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a firefighter and put out big fires.

halaman.alt: The girl wears a nurse's cap. She holds up her teddy and presses a stethoscope up to its heart.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a nurse and make sick people better.

halaman.alt: The girl plays a guitar.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a musician and play in a band.

halaman.alt: The girl holds out a spanner. There is a toy car in the corner.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a mechanic and fix cars and tractors.

halaman.alt: The girl writes the alphabet on a chalkboard.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a teacher and teach children to read and write.

halaman.alt: The girl wears soccer boots and socks and kicks a soccer ball.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a soccer player and score the winning goal.

halaman.alt: The girl wears a space suit. The moon is behind her.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be an astronaut and fly to the moon.

halaman.alt: The girl wears a chef's hat and licks her fingers. There is a pile of biscuits in the corner.
teks: When I grow up, I want to be a chef and make food for my family and friends.

halaman.alt: The girl holds her sunflower and dreams of being a ballet dancer, an astronaut and a teacher.
teks: When I grow up, I can choose whatever I want to be!

halaman.alt: A collage of ballet shoes, biscuits, a chalkboard, a toy car, a guitar, a fireman's hat, a teddy, a soccer ball and the moon.
teks: What do you want to be when you grow up?

buku.title: Who is our friend?
buku.creator: Gerhard Van Wyk, Jade Mathieson, Lara de Groot
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Rhino, Crocodile, Giraffe and Zebra all have an unlikely friend. Can you guess who he is?

halaman.alt: Crocodile, Zebra, Giraffe and Rhino stand together.
teks: Can you guess who our best friend is?
He’s not like us at all.

halaman.alt: Bird sits alone.
teks: Our best friend is Bird!

halaman.alt: Rhino snorts angrily at the fleas buzzing around his tail.
teks: I am Rhino.
I get covered in fleas.

halaman.alt: Bird sits on Rhino's back with a fly in his beak. Rhino is happy.
teks: Bird eats them all up.

halaman.alt: Crocodile opens his mouth to show his rows of teeth.
teks: I am Crocodile.
I can’t brush my teeth.

halaman.alt: Bird sits in Crocodile's mouth and pecks at his teeth.
teks: Bird pecks them all clean.

halaman.alt: Giraffe tries to curl his tongue out behind him.
teks: I am Giraffe.
I can’t scratch my head.

halaman.alt: Bird perches on Giraffe's neck and holds a small twig.
teks: Bird can reach just the right spot.

halaman.alt: Zebra stands in the tall grass and squints.
teks: I am Zebra.
I can’t see things far away.

halaman.alt: Bird sits on Zebra's head and looks out into the distance. Zebra is happy.
teks: Bird has great eyes,
so when he’s watching I’m safe.

halaman.alt: The animals stand together. Only their legs are visible. Bird is on the ground.
teks: Bird might be different, but that’s no problem...

halaman.alt: Bird sings loudly. The animals watch.
teks: We don’t even mind when he sings!
Will you be my friend?

buku.title: Whose button is this?
buku.creator: Paul Kennedy, James Woolley, Louise Gale
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Tinny Tim sets out on an adventure to return a lost button. Along the way he goes exploring, has a miraculous escape, and makes new friends.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim is a toy robot. A blue button bounces up to him.
teks: Tinny Tim was sitting on the road when a button bounced his way.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim carries the button. He walks with determination.
teks: “I wonder where this comes from,” he said.
He wanted to find out.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim almost gets squashed under someone's red shoe.
teks: It was busy on the side of the road.
“Woah!”
He nearly got squashed.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim holds onto the shoe lace. He swings through the air.
teks: He made a lucky escape.
“It’s scary out here,” he said.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim looks up to the green man on the traffic light.
teks: “Hey there, is this yours?”

halaman.alt: The green man changes to a red man.
teks: The green man said nothing. He just turned red.
“What a rude person.”

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim sees a dog in the distance.
teks: Tinny Tim carried on looking.
“Whose button is this?”

halaman.alt: The dog licks Tinny Tim. He gets covered in dog drool.
teks: “Woah..!
...at least he’s friendly.”

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim holds the button. He stands at a pedestrian crossing.
teks: “I’ve got to get to the other side.
I’m sure that’s where this comes from.”

halaman.alt: A car drives through a puddle and he gets splashed.
teks: SPLASH!
“That was close.”
He waited for the cars to pass before he carried on.

halaman.alt: Tinny Tim holds the button in the air.
teks: Maybe this was who he was looking for.
“Hello, who are you?”

halaman.alt: Ruby Rags is a doll with buttons for eyes. She is missing one eye.
teks: “I’m Ruby Rags.” “I think this is yours,”he said.

halaman.alt: Ruby Rags and Tinny Tim sit next to each other. Ruby has both eyes!
teks: “Thank you, little robot. Can we be friends?”

buku.title: Why is Nita upside down?
buku.creator: Emma Hearne, Roxana Bouwer, Sarah Bouwer
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: Nita’s hanging upside down. Can she turn the right way round?

halaman.alt: Nita hangs upside down from a jungle gym.
teks: Nita’s hanging upside down, her long hair tickling at the ground.
The trees, the grass, the everything is all the wrong way round.

halaman.alt: Navi walks through the play area and waves.
teks: Her feet, they poke into the sky. Little Navi’s walking by.
He says ‘I’ve seen you here before. You’re upside down again! What for?’

halaman.alt: Nita speaks through a broken speech bubble.
teks: His feet swim lightly in the air. She tries to hide behind her hair.
‘It’s h-h-h-hard to t-t-talk’, she says to him. ‘I’m not the same. I don’t fit in.

halaman.alt: Navi's look-out spot is a tall tree.
teks: Navi takes her by the hand. He wants to help her understand.
They climb to Navi’s look-out spot. From up here they can see a lot.
They perch and have a quiet stare at children playing here and there.

halaman.alt: There are children playing on a slide, swings, a seesaw and a merry-go-round.
An overweight boy holds a stick. A girl with freckled cheeks sucks a lolly pop.
teks: Those kids are not the same at all.
Abe’s round.
Chi's freckled.

halaman.alt: Lala is a girl with very long legs.
teks: Lala’s extra tall.

halaman.alt: A boy runs and jumps with his hands in the air. A girl reads a book.
teks: Bambam’s wild and must be free, while Lulu's reading quietly.

halaman.alt: A girl with long bushy hair swings on the swing.
teks: Look at Freya's crazy hair.

halaman.alt: A boy wearing spectacles tries to shoot a catapult.
teks: And Sid wears glasses everywhere.

halaman.alt: Nita and Navi sit on a branch.
teks: And me, I am just skin and bone.
And you are you. You’re not alone.
Each human’s sort of strange, you see. That makes you just the same, like me.
This world is really one big game. To play, we can’t all be the same.

halaman.alt: Nita stands up straight and smiles.
teks: Nita feels the right way round, thanks to the new friend she's found.
Upside down was never fun.
Now she plays with everyone.

buku.title: Zanele Situ: My Story
buku.subtitle: The Story of Zanele Situ
buku.creator: Liz Sparg, Jesse Breytenbach, Andy Thesen
buku.subject: Juvenile Fiction
buku.description: As a young girl Zanele Situ was told that she would never walk again. Being in a wheelchair did not stop her. She worked and trained hard and became a winning athlete on the world stage. This is her story…

halaman.alt: A young and healthy Zanele plays outside with her father. Her mother looks on.
teks: I was born in summer, in a town called Matatiele in the Eastern Cape. Matatiele is near Lesotho where there are many mountains. In the winter they are covered with snow.

halaman.alt: Zanele lies in a hospital bed. Her mother is worried. The doctor explains that something is wrong with Zanele.
teks: My father was a builder and he moved from place to place to find work. We moved to Lesotho and that's where I started school. I was very happy. But when I was eleven years old, I grew tired and weak, and then I couldn't walk. My parents took me to the hospital.

halaman.alt: Zanele lies in the hospital bed. The doctor brings a wheelchair. He says that Zanele has TB in her spine.
teks: I had to stay in hospital for three years. I was very tired and I slept many hours every day. After three years the doctors told me I would not be able to walk again. I was very sad because I love sports.

halaman.alt: Zanele sits outside in her wheelchair. A sports coach holds a javelin in front of her. He asks her how far she can throw it.
teks: I went to a special school in Umtata, and my teachers encouraged me. It was a very busy school, with lots of activities like sport and sewing. On weekends we had tasks to do. We had to clean our rooms, polish our shoes and clean our wheelchairs.

halaman.alt: Zanele practises throwing things from her wheelchair. Eventually she throws the javelin.
teks: I decided to keep trying, and never give up. If you have a disability, you can still do something you love. I love to see how far I can go, so I entered a competition. I won a bronze medal for shot putt, a silver medal for discus and a gold medal for javelin.

halaman.alt: Zanele lifts weights in her wheelchair. Her coach encourages her. Zanele sews and listens to music on the radio.
teks: I wanted to get better and better at my sports, so I trained very hard.
When I rested, I loved to sew and listen to gospel music.

halaman.alt: Zanele receives a trophy. She dreams of winning at the Paralympics.
teks: I entered more competitions and I got many medals and prizes. I started to dream about maybe competing in the Paralympics one day.

halaman.alt: At the Paralympics disabled sportsmen and women parade with their national flags . Zanele holds the South African flag.
teks: The Paralympics are just like the Olympics, where the best athletes in the world compete for gold, silver and bronze medals.
But in the Paralympics, the athletes are disabled in different ways, so they have to try even harder to train and win!

halaman.alt: Zanele sits on an aeroplane. She is excited.
teks: Then I heard that I was going to Sydney in Australia, to take part in the 2000 Paralympics. At last we were in the plane, flying over the Indian Ocean!

halaman.alt: Zanele sits in her wheelchair. She looks at the enormous sports field.
teks: But when I got there, I suddenly felt very scared of all the people watching me. I just wanted to go home again.

halaman.alt: Zanele throws the javelin from her wheelchair.
teks: Then, when I threw my javelin it landed far in front of everyone's. I broke the world record and I got a gold medal! I was the first African woman to win a gold medal in the Paralympics. I was so happy and very proud.

halaman.alt: Zanele wears her medal around her neck. She hugs her young daughter from her wheelchair.
teks: My motto is: Keep going, follow your dreams and never give up. Even if something happens to make you sad or scared.
That is what I teach my little girl, Azamazi. She is eight years old and she also loves to do athletics and gymnastics.
I am still training and going to competitions, and in 2016 I hope to go to the Paralympics in Rio de Janeiro.
